title: Beware the EdTech Industry Rebrand: Part 2
author: Emily and Denise
summary: In the second installment of their 'Reckoning' series, Emily and Denise dissect ISTE's newly released 'Summary of Evidence for Technology in Education' report as a textbook case of what they call 'screenwashing' — borrowing the term from 'greenwashing' to describe an industry-funded attempt to look more socially responsible than it is. They walk through what they call ISTE's four-step 'screenwashing playbook' (flatten concerns to 'screentime,' claim EdTech is different from consumer tech, frame grassroots pushback as extreme, and cite unrepresentative 'rare-use' cases), noting that ISTE's report is funded by Google and Meta. The piece's strongest evidence comes from close-reading ISTE's own cited sources: a study meant to show 'poorly built EdTech' harms learning actually concludes that digital reading in general underperforms paper, and a separate industry report meant to distinguish quality EdTech from consumer tech reveals only 2% of the products it reviewed show strong evidence of effectiveness under the federal ESSA framework. The authors also flag a $23 million partnership between OpenAI, Microsoft, and the American Federation of Teachers to fund an 'AI Instruction' academy as part of the same pattern — criticize teachers for misusing the product, then position yourself as the trainer who fixes it. The piece ends with a call to action for parents and teachers to organize against EdTech industry messaging ahead of the new school year.
points: The authors define 'screenwashing' as an industry playbook — flatten concerns to 'screentime,' claim EdTech is meaningfully different from consumer tech, frame grassroots pushback as extremist, and cite rare or unrepresentative use cases — and argue ISTE's new report follows it step by step.

Their strongest single piece of evidence: the study ISTE cites to argue that only 'poorly built' EdTech harms learning (Stole et al., 2020) actually concludes that digital reading underperforms paper reading generally, which doesn't support ISTE's quality-differentiation claim at all.

A separate industry report (Instructure's) that ISTE-aligned messaging relies on to distinguish 'EdTech' from 'consumer tech' shows only 2% of reviewed EdTech products meet the federal ESSA standard for strong evidence of effectiveness.

The piece connects a $23 million OpenAI/Microsoft-funded partnership with the American Federation of Teachers (to build a 'National Academy of AI Instruction') to the same pattern: blame teachers for poor implementation, then become the paid trainer who 'fixes' it.
quotes: The backlash to EdTech is not actually about "screentime" (too much vs. too little). The backlash is in response to the fact that the business model of Big Tech and EdTech companies is in direct conflict with healthy child development.

First, ISTE considers Google and Meta both proud funding sponsors and partners. That alone should stop anyone genuinely concerned about children's use of such products from reading the rest of the document.

Our finding that students across all skill levels perform more poorly on a digital test than on paper, is an urgent call for a more nuanced perspective on implementation of digital technologies in elementary education, and a signal to policy makers, school administrators and educators that the medium matters, especially for reading comprehension.

A troubling divide is emerging: mass, app-based instruction for the many, and human tutoring and intellectual exchange reserved for the elite. What is sold as the 'democratisation' of education may be entrenching further inequality.

Looking deeper into Instructure's report we see that only 40% of what they deem as the "top EdTech tools" they analyzed have any level of ESSA evidence and even worse, the majority have only Tier 3 which describes research that shows "promising evidence" and Tier 4 isn't even research - it's a rationale!
This "groundbreaking $23 million education initiative" will provide access to "free AI training and curriculum for all 1.8 million members of the AFT, starting with K-12 educators.

These companies are worried, as evidenced by the hate mail and death threats we've both gotten for speaking up and out about this. But it's because they know we are right, and they see the pushback growing from all over the world.
